title: Top bar navigation
use_when: Five or fewer top-level destinations, content-first pages, public or marketing surfaces where a persistent side rail would steal width.
avoid_when: Deep hierarchies with many peer sections, admin tools that need permanent wayfinding, or anything on TV.
guidance: Put primary destinations in a single horizontal bar; collapse to a menu button below the container width rather than hiding destinations one by one. The active item must be marked by more than colour (underline, weight, or aria-current). On narrow widths, the bar keeps the brand mark and one primary action visible.

implementation.react: Use a <nav aria-label="Primary"> with <a aria-current="page">; collapse via a disclosure button that toggles aria-expanded, not CSS-only hover.
implementation.html-css: <header><nav aria-label=Primary><ul>…; use :has() or a checkbox-free JS toggle for the collapsed menu.

source: Common web practice; WAI-ARIA APG navigation patterns

title: Persistent left rail / sidebar
use_when: Authenticated tools with 6+ peer sections, frequent switching, and wide viewports; power users who need stable wayfinding.
avoid_when: Marketing pages, single-task flows (checkout, onboarding), phone widths, or when the product has three destinations and the rail would be mostly empty.
guidance: Fixed-width rail (collapsible to icons with labels on hover/focus) holding grouped sections; secondary navigation lives in the content header, not as a second rail. Don't add a rail because 'apps have sidebars': justify it with section count and switching frequency. Mark active section with a visible indicator that survives collapse.

implementation.shadcn: Use the Sidebar primitives (SidebarProvider/SidebarMenu) which already handle collapse state and keyboard; do not hand-roll a second implementation.
implementation.winui: NavigationView with PaneDisplayMode=Auto handles collapse and access keys; put page-level commands in a CommandBar, not the pane.
implementation.wpf: Left ListBox/TreeView bound to view models with IsSynchronizedWithCurrentItem; ensure KeyboardNavigation.TabNavigation=Once so Tab leaves the rail in one press.

source: Windows NavigationView guidance; common SaaS practice

title: Bottom tab bar
use_when: Phone apps with 3–5 top-level destinations of similar importance that users switch between often.
avoid_when: More than five destinations, tablet/desktop widths (use a rail), single-flow apps, or when one destination dominates usage.
guidance: 3–5 items, icon + label always (no icon-only), safe-area aware, current item indicated by more than tint. Each tab keeps its own navigation stack. Don't put actions (compose, add) in the tab bar unless it is the app's primary action and it is styled as an action, not a destination.

implementation.compose: NavigationBar + NavigationBarItem with label always shown; scaffold with contentWindowInsets so the bar respects gesture-nav insets.
implementation.swiftui: TabView with Label(text, systemImage); avoid custom bars unless brand requires, since the system bar handles Dynamic Type and VoiceOver.
implementation.flutter: NavigationBar (M3) or CupertinoTabBar; keep per-tab Navigator state.
implementation.react-native: @react-navigation/bottom-tabs with tabBarLabel visible; set accessibilityRole on custom items.

source: Apple HIG Tab bars; Material 3 Navigation bar

title: Hub and spoke
use_when: Infrequent, distinct tasks (pay a bill, book a slot, check a reading) where users come in for one job and leave; kiosks and public-service apps.
avoid_when: Frequent switching between areas, browsing/discovery products, or dense tools.
guidance: One home screen of large, labelled entry points; each spoke is a linear flow with an obvious way back to the hub. Group entry points by user goal, not by internal system module. On kiosks, the hub also serves as the idle/attract screen and every spoke must time out back to it.
source: Common practice in banking, government and kiosk apps

title: TV side navigation (collapsible drawer)
use_when: TV apps with 4–8 sections (Home, Live, Movies, Series, Search, Settings) where the vertical axis is free for section switching and the horizontal axis is used for browsing rails.
avoid_when: Two or three sections (use top tabs), single-purpose players, or when content rails need the full width and the drawer would fight with left-edge focus.
guidance: Collapsed icon strip on the left that expands to icons+labels when focus enters it; pressing LEFT from the first item of any rail moves focus into the drawer, RIGHT returns to the last focused content item (focus restoration is mandatory). Back from content returns to the drawer, Back from the drawer exits or goes Home. Never require UP to reach navigation from deep in a page.

implementation.compose-tv: NavigationDrawer/ModalNavigationDrawer from androidx.tv.material3; wrap content in focusRestorer() so RIGHT returns to the previous item; give the drawer a focusGroup.
implementation.react-native: Use TVFocusGuideView with destinations to route LEFT from rails into the drawer; keep hasTVPreferredFocus on the last content item.
implementation.swiftui: tvOS: TabView with .tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable) provides the system sidebar; do not rebuild it.

source: Android TV design: Navigation drawer; Android TV navigation-on-tv guide

title: TV top tabs
use_when: Two to five sections, when the left edge must stay free for immersive artwork or when the brand wants a browsing feel closer to a broadcast guide.
avoid_when: More than five sections, or when rows below are long (UP from deep rows must scroll back to tabs predictably; that gets slow).
guidance: Tabs sit in the top safe area; Back from any rail jumps focus to the active tab and scrolls to top; focused tab shows the underline/pill with ≥3:1 contrast and the label stays visible. Switching tabs does not move focus into content until the user presses DOWN.

implementation.compose-tv: TabRow from androidx.tv.material3 with focusRestorer(); handle BackHandler to move focus back to the selected tab.
implementation.swiftui: tvOS TabView default style renders top tabs; use .focusSection() on content groups.

source: Android TV design: Tabs; Navigation on TV (back returns to top nav)

title: Command palette as primary navigation accelerator
use_when: Power-user tools with many commands/records; users who live on the keyboard; anywhere a menu tree would be three levels deep.
avoid_when: Touch-first products, casual users, or as the only way to reach a feature (it augments visible navigation, never replaces it).
guidance: Global shortcut (Ctrl/Cmd+K), fuzzy search over commands and records, recent items first, arrow-key navigation with aria-activedescendant, Escape closes and restores focus. Every command in the palette must also exist somewhere visible.

implementation.shadcn: Command (cmdk) component; register commands centrally so menus and palette share one source.
implementation.winui: Implement as a ContentDialog-free Flyout with an AutoSuggestBox; register KeyboardAccelerator on the root.
implementation.wpf: Popup + ListBox with VirtualizingStackPanel; InputBindings for the global gesture.

source: Linear, VS Code, Raycast conventions; WAI-ARIA combobox pattern

title: Tree + breadcrumb for deep hierarchies
use_when: Hierarchies of 3+ levels (accounts → cost centres → entries, folders, org charts) where users need to see where they are and jump laterally.
avoid_when: Flat structures, mobile widths, or when the tree would exceed a few hundred visible nodes without virtualisation.
guidance: Tree in the left pane with full keyboard semantics (arrow keys expand/collapse, type-ahead), breadcrumb above the content that mirrors the tree path and is clickable at every level. Persist expansion state per session. Virtualise beyond ~500 nodes.

implementation.winui: TreeView with ItemsSource + BreadcrumbBar; both are accessible out of the box.
implementation.react: Use a tested tree (react-arborist, or a headless treeview following the APG pattern) rather than nested <ul> with click handlers.

title: Linear wizard / stepper
use_when: One task with ordered dependent steps (checkout, onboarding, application forms) where finishing matters more than exploring.
avoid_when: Steps are independent and users need to jump around (use tabs or a form with sections), or the whole thing fits on one screen.
guidance: Show step count and current step, allow going back without data loss, put one primary action per step, validate per step not at the end, and let completed steps be revisited. Save progress for flows longer than ~3 minutes. On TV, each step is a full screen with a single focused default action.
source: Nielsen Norman Group wizard guidance; GOV.UK one-thing-per-page

title: Desktop menu bar + toolbar commands
use_when: Document-centric or record-centric desktop apps with many commands, where discoverability through menus and accelerators matters (Alt+F, Ctrl+S).
avoid_when: Consumer apps with a handful of actions (use a command bar), touch-first devices, or web apps pretending to be native.
guidance: Menu bar for the complete command set with access keys and accelerators shown; toolbar/command bar for the frequent subset; context menus mirror the toolbar for the selected object. Commands must be enabled/disabled by state, never hidden, so users learn where things live.

implementation.winui: MenuBar + CommandBar; assign KeyboardAccelerator and AccessKey on every MenuFlyoutItem.
implementation.wpf: Menu/ToolBar bound to ICommand with InputGestureText; RoutedUICommand gives free accelerators.
implementation.avalonia: NativeMenu on macOS, Menu on Windows/Linux; HotKey on MenuItem.

source: Windows app design: menus and context menus; macOS HIG menus

title: Single column, one task
use_when: Phone screens, forms, reading, onboarding, kiosks: one primary thing per screen.
avoid_when: Comparison tasks, dense data, or wide desktop windows where a single narrow column wastes the viewport and forces scrolling.
guidance: Content width capped for reading (~60–75 characters per line), vertical rhythm from the spacing scale, primary action reachable without scrolling on the shortest supported viewport, or sticky at the bottom.

title: Master–detail (list + detail pane)
use_when: Users scan a list of records and act on one at a time (tickets, orders, patients, mail); wide enough for two panes (≥ ~900 px / 641 epx).
avoid_when: Phone widths (collapse to list → push detail), records that need the full width (large tables, editors), or when the list has only a handful of items.
guidance: List pane with selection state that is keyboard-navigable (arrow keys change selection, Enter opens), detail pane that updates in place and announces its title to assistive tech. Persist the selected item across navigation. On narrow widths collapse to a two-screen stack with Back.

implementation.winui: Two-column Grid with a splitter, or the WinUI Gallery master/detail sample; ListView.SelectionMode=Single with SelectedItem bound TwoWay.
implementation.swiftui: NavigationSplitView handles collapse on compact size classes.
implementation.react: Route the selected id in the URL so detail is deep-linkable and Back works.

source: Windows list/details pattern; Material adaptive list-detail; Apple NavigationSplitView

title: Three-pane workbench
use_when: Navigation tree + list + editor/inspector workflows (mail clients, IDE-like tools, CMS, ledgers) on ≥1280 px windows.
avoid_when: Anything below laptop width, casual products, or when the third pane is mostly empty.
guidance: Resizable panes with remembered sizes, each pane a landmark/region with a heading, F6-style pane cycling on desktop, collapse order defined (inspector collapses first). Keyboard focus must be able to move between panes without tabbing through every control.

implementation.winui: Grid with GridSplitter (CommunityToolkit); SplitView for the outer pane.
implementation.wpf: Grid with GridSplitter; persist column widths in settings.
implementation.react: react-resizable-panels or CSS grid with a splitter; each pane gets role=region and aria-label.

title: Dashboard grid of modules
use_when: Monitoring/overview screens where several independent modules (KPIs, charts, lists) are scanned together and ranked by importance.
avoid_when: Task screens (forms, editors), narrow widths (stack instead), or when modules have no ordering logic and would be a wall of equal boxes.
guidance: 12-column responsive grid, modules sized by importance (the primary KPI or chart spans wider), reading order = importance order (top-left first), each module a region with a heading and its own loading/empty/error states. Cards are optional: a divider grid with headings is often clearer than nested boxes.
source: Dashboard design literature (Few, Information Dashboard Design)

title: Table-first working screen
use_when: The record set is the product (orders, transactions, tickets, inventory): users filter, sort, select, and bulk-act. Screen = toolbar + filters + table + optional side panel.
avoid_when: Phone widths (switch to list rows), fewer than ~20 rows, or when each record needs rich media.
guidance: Table fills the viewport height with internal scrolling and sticky header, row density selectable, column widths persisted, filters as a row of chips/fields above the table (not a hidden drawer), bulk actions appear in the toolbar on selection. Numeric columns right-aligned with tabular figures. Virtualise beyond a few hundred rows.

implementation.react: TanStack Table for logic + TanStack Virtual for rows; render <table> semantics or role=grid with aria-rowcount.
implementation.winui: DataGrid from CommunityToolkit or a virtualised ListView with a header; enable IsItemClickEnabled and keyboard sorting.
implementation.wpf: DataGrid with EnableRowVirtualization and VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping; DevExpress GridControl if already present.
implementation.avalonia: DataGrid (Avalonia.Controls.DataGrid) or TreeDataGrid for large sets.

source: Enterprise data table conventions; WAI-ARIA grid pattern

title: Form stack with sections
use_when: Data entry and settings: labelled fields in one column, grouped into titled sections, with the save/submit action fixed in a predictable place.
avoid_when: Spreadsheet-style batch entry (use a data-entry grid), or tiny forms of 1–2 fields (inline them).
guidance: Labels above fields (not placeholders), one column except for tightly related pairs (city/postcode), section headings as real headings, inline validation on blur with error text linked via aria-describedby, and the primary action at the end of the form or in a sticky footer. Field width should hint expected length.
source: GOV.UK Design System forms; Luke Wroblewski Web Form Design

title: Catalog grid
use_when: Browsing many visually distinguishable items (products, courses, photos) where the image is the primary recognition cue.
avoid_when: Items with no meaningful image, dense attribute comparison (use a table), or TV (use rails).
guidance: Responsive columns from a minimum tile width (auto-fill/minmax), consistent aspect ratio per catalog, text under the image not over it unless contrast is guaranteed, and a filter/sort bar that stays reachable. Lazy-load images with reserved aspect boxes to avoid layout shift.
source: E-commerce PLP conventions; CSS Grid auto-fill

title: Vertical feed
use_when: Chronological or ranked streams of heterogeneous items (posts, notifications, activity) consumed by scrolling.
avoid_when: Users need to find a specific item (add search/filters or use a table), or the items are homogeneous records (use a list/table).
guidance: One column, items separated by dividers or spacing rather than each wrapped in a card, actions per item revealed consistently, infinite scroll with a visible 'load more' fallback and a way to return to top. Preserve scroll position on back navigation.

title: Editorial columns
use_when: Long-form reading, articles, documentation, brand storytelling: a measured text column with asymmetric side content (figures, pull quotes, table of contents).
avoid_when: Applications, dashboards, anything users operate rather than read.
guidance: Primary column 60–75 characters wide, generous line height, figures can break the measure, headings carry the rhythm. A sticky table of contents on wide screens, none on narrow. Resist a hero banner unless the page is a landing page; an article starts with its title.

title: Horizontal rails (rows of content)
use_when: TV browsing of categorised content: vertical axis moves between categories, horizontal axis moves within a category. The default TV home structure.
avoid_when: Fewer than ~8 items total (use a grid or list), or content that must be compared side by side.
guidance: Each rail has a visible title, focused item scrolls to a fixed pivot (about 20–30% from the left) rather than centring, rails remember their last focused index when returning, row heights are consistent within a rail, and off-screen items are partially visible to signal continuation. Lazy-load rails and images; never render every rail on first paint. Keep the safe margin (~5% / 48 dp horizontal, 27 dp vertical at 960×540 dp).

implementation.compose-tv: LazyColumn of LazyRow (Compose Foundation ≥1.7 has focus-aware scrolling); wrap each row in focusRestorer(); set LocalBringIntoViewSpec for the pivot; TvLazyRow is deprecated.
implementation.react-native: FlatList horizontal with initialNumToRender small; TVFocusGuideView per rail; keep a ref of last focused index.
implementation.swiftui: tvOS: ScrollView(.horizontal) with LazyHStack and .focusSection(); use .scrollTargetLayout for pivot behaviour.
implementation.react: Web-on-TV: implement spatial navigation (e.g. @noriginmedia/norigin-spatial-navigation) with per-rail focus memory; CSS scroll-snap alone is not enough.

source: Android TV layouts guide (safe margins, card widths); Navigation on TV (axis rules); Compose for TV lists guide

title: Immersive hero + rails
use_when: Media apps that want the focused item's artwork to fill the background while rails sit below; strongest when artwork quality is high and consistent.
avoid_when: Poor or inconsistent artwork, catalogues where text metadata matters more than imagery, or low-end devices where large image decode causes jank.
guidance: Backdrop crossfades on focus change with a debounce (~300 ms) so scrubbing across a rail doesn't thrash decodes; a scrim gradient guarantees text contrast over any image; the hero text block sits in the safe area with title, one line of metadata, and a short synopsis; the first rail is partially visible so users know to press DOWN. Provide a reduced-motion path with a static backdrop.

implementation.compose-tv: ImmersiveList is deprecated; build with a Box(backdrop AsyncImage with Crossfade) + LazyColumn; use snapshotFlow on focused item with debounce.
implementation.react-native: Animated.Image with opacity transition; preload next/prev backdrops; cap backdrop resolution to panel size.

source: Android TV design: Immersive list / Featured carousel; Compose for TV samples (JetStream)

title: Player with overlay controls
use_when: Full-screen playback with transient controls (scrub, play/pause, next, subtitles, quality) that appear on input and hide on inactivity.
avoid_when: Never for non-media; for audio-only use a persistent mini-player instead.
guidance: Controls overlay with a scrim, show on any key/tap/mouse move, hide after ~3–5 s of inactivity but never while a control has focus or a menu is open; first focus lands on play/pause; LEFT/RIGHT seek with visible thumbnail/time; subtitles and audio selection in a side sheet that pauses the auto-hide; the progress bar is a real slider with keyboard/remote semantics and a text time readout.

implementation.compose-tv: Media3 PlayerView or a custom Compose overlay; handle KEYCODE_MEDIA_* and DPAD_CENTER; use focusRequester to land on play/pause.
implementation.react-native: react-native-video + custom overlay; TVEventHandler for play/pause/select.
implementation.html-css: <video> with custom controls following the APG slider pattern; keep native controls as fallback.

source: Android TV playback guidance; Apple tvOS HIG playback

title: EPG / program guide grid
use_when: Live TV channel × time grids with a 'now' line, current programme highlighted, and channel logos in a fixed column.
avoid_when: On-demand catalogues (use rails), or phone portrait (use a per-channel list).
guidance: Two-dimensional virtualisation (channels vertical, time horizontal), sticky channel column and time header, programme cells sized by duration with a minimum width so short programmes stay focusable, current time line always visible, LEFT/RIGHT move within a channel's programmes (not by pixel), UP/DOWN keep the same time slot, long press or a shortcut jumps to now, focused cell shows full title + time in a detail strip rather than truncating inside the cell.

implementation.compose-tv: Custom LazyLayout or a LazyRow of LazyColumn with shared scroll state; do not use nested LazyRows per channel without a shared time offset.
implementation.react: Planby-style engine: absolutely positioned cells within a virtualised window; spatial navigation must resolve by cell, not by geometry alone.
implementation.react-native: Virtualise both axes yourself; FlatList alone will not handle time-based cell widths.

source: Broadcast EPG conventions; Android TV Live tab guidance

title: High density
use_when: Expert users, repeated daily use, comparison and scanning tasks, large screens with a pointer.
avoid_when: Touch-only, first-time users, TV, or emotional/branding surfaces.
guidance: 4 px base grid, 32 px row height in tables, 13–14 px body, 8–12 px gaps inside groups and 16–24 px between groups; density must be achieved by tightening spacing and sizes coherently, not by shrinking text below the platform floor. Offer a 'comfortable' density toggle where users differ.
source: Windows content spacing (4 epx grid); Material density guidance

title: Medium density
use_when: General-purpose apps, mixed audiences, touch and pointer both supported.
avoid_when: Extremes: expert data tools (go high) or brand storytelling (go low).
guidance: 8 px base, 40–48 px interactive heights, 16 px body on web/mobile, 16 px inside groups and 24–32 px between groups. This is the safe default when the audience is unknown; state that it was a default.

title: Low density / spacious
use_when: Marketing, storytelling, reading, TV (viewing distance), kiosks (public, hurried users), luxury/brand-led products.
avoid_when: Operational tools where scrolling to see the next row costs time.
guidance: Whitespace must come from a scale (e.g. 24/40/64/96), not arbitrary padding; keep line length in measure; big type is only justified for the one thing that should be read first. Spacious does not mean everything is huge.

title: Flat surfaces with tonal layers
use_when: Most application UI: hierarchy expressed with subtle background tone steps (canvas → surface → elevated) and dividers rather than shadows on everything.
avoid_when: When physical elevation carries meaning (floating menus, dragged items) it still needs a shadow; don't flatten those.
guidance: Define three tonal steps per theme with measured contrast (each step ≥1.1:1 apart and borders ≥3:1 where they mark boundaries). Shadows reserved for transient layers (menus, dialogs, drag). Reads professional at any density and avoids the 'everything is a floating card' look.

title: Bordered panes
use_when: Dense workbenches where regions are separated by 1 px borders and the canvas is a single tone; the IDE/spreadsheet aesthetic.
avoid_when: Consumer or brand-led products, touch-first products with fat targets.
guidance: One neutral canvas, borders with ≥3:1 contrast where they define panes, headers as slightly darker/lighter strips, no rounded card containers inside panes. Focus rings and selection highlights carry the colour.
source: Desktop workbench conventions (IDEs, spreadsheets, Windows Explorer)

title: Elevated cards as the primary container
use_when: Each item is a self-contained, tappable object (a product, a post, a course) and the card boundary is also the touch target.
avoid_when: Dashboards and tables (cards inside cards), text-heavy content, dense desktop tools, or when the card contains a single line of text.
guidance: One elevation level for resting cards, one for pressed/dragged; the whole card is the target with a single accessible name; never nest a card inside a card; cards in a grid share aspect ratio and padding. If more than ~30% of a screen is card borders, switch to dividers.

title: Imagery-backed surfaces
use_when: Content whose artwork is the brand (film, music, fashion): backgrounds and cards are the images themselves with scrims for text.
avoid_when: Inconsistent or user-generated imagery, data screens, or when text must be reliably readable without scrims.
guidance: Every text-over-image placement gets a scrim tuned so the worst-case image still yields ≥4.5:1; image sizes are capped to the panel/viewport; focus/hover states cannot rely on colour changes hidden by imagery (use scale, border, glow). Provide a text-only fallback for missing artwork.
source: Streaming app conventions; Android TV Immersive list

title: Translucent (glass) layers, justified
use_when: Only where a transient layer must show what is beneath it (media overlays, system-style sheets on iOS/macOS/Windows Mica) and the platform provides the material natively.
avoid_when: Cards, panels, or backgrounds in application UI; anything on TV or low-end devices; wherever text sits on unpredictable content beneath.
guidance: Use the platform material (UIVisualEffectView, Mica/Acrylic, backdrop-filter with a solid fallback) rather than a hand-made blur; verify contrast against the darkest and lightest content that can appear behind; measure frame cost. If glass is chosen for brand reasons, say so and limit it to one surface type.

title: Neutral workhorse sans
use_when: Dense, functional UI where the type must disappear: tables, forms, consoles. Prioritise x-height, tabular figures, and broad language coverage.
avoid_when: Brand-led or editorial products where the type is part of the identity (this choice will read as default).
guidance: One family with tabular figures and a wide weight range (e.g. IBM Plex Sans, Source Sans 3, Public Sans, Atkinson Hyperlegible, or the platform system font). Display role uses the same family at heavier weight and tighter tracking rather than a second face. If the codebase already uses a system font, keep it.

title: Platform system font
use_when: Native apps that should feel at home (SF on Apple, Roboto/Google Sans on Android/TV, Segoe UI Variable on Windows); products where Dynamic Type/text scaling and rendering quality matter more than distinctiveness.
avoid_when: Multi-brand products that need differentiation, or web where 'system-ui' varies unpredictably across OSes.
guidance: Use the platform text styles (Dynamic Type styles, Material type roles, Windows type ramp) so scaling, weights, and optical sizes are correct for free; add brand through colour, layout, and one display accent if needed.

implementation.swiftui: Font.title/.body etc.; never fixed point sizes for body text.
implementation.compose: MaterialTheme.typography; for TV use androidx.tv.material3 typography (larger scale).
implementation.winui: TextBlock Style={StaticResource BodyTextBlockStyle} and the other ramp styles; Segoe UI Variable via the default theme.

source: Apple HIG Typography; Material type scale; Windows typography

title: Humanist sans for approachable products
use_when: Consumer or public-service products where warmth and legibility for broad audiences matter; long forms; multilingual content.
avoid_when: Tech/luxury brands wanting a sharp identity, or when the product already uses a geometric face consistently.
guidance: Open apertures and generous x-height (e.g. Source Sans 3, Nunito Sans, Open Sans, Fira Sans, Noto Sans for coverage). Pair with a slightly heavier weight for headings rather than a second family unless brand demands it.

title: Geometric sans for product/tech brands
use_when: Startup/tech identity, product marketing, consumer apps wanting a modern, constructed feel.
avoid_when: Dense tables (geometric faces often lack tabular figures and have low x-height), or when the whole category already uses the same one or two faces (Inter, Space Grotesk, Poppins are now default-looking).
guidance: Choose a face the category is not saturated with (e.g. Manrope, Outfit, Urbanist, Sora, Figtree, Plus Jakarta Sans, Albert Sans, Geist for dev tools) and verify numerals and weights. Use the display cut only for the largest role.

title: Grotesk display + quiet body
use_when: Brand-led surfaces where a characterful display face at large sizes carries identity while a neutral body face does the reading work.
avoid_when: Applications where display sizes rarely appear, or when performance budgets cannot afford a second web font.
guidance: Display face with real character (e.g. Bricolage Grotesque, Instrument Sans, Familjen Grotesk, Schibsted Grotesk, Unbounded for very bold) used at ≥28 px only; body from a proven text face. Subset and preload the display font; on TV keep the display weight heavy enough to survive overscan and compression.

title: Serif editorial text
use_when: Long reading, journalism, essays, premium financial or legal content where a text serif improves reading rhythm and signals authority.
avoid_when: Operational UI, small labels, TV (serifs degrade at distance/compression), dark backgrounds at small sizes.
guidance: A text serif with optical sizes (e.g. Source Serif 4, Literata, Newsreader, Fraunces for display, Spectral) at 17–19 px body with 1.5–1.6 line height; UI chrome (buttons, labels) stays in a sans to keep controls crisp.

title: Serif display accent
use_when: Luxury, fashion, hospitality, culture: a high-contrast serif for headlines only, everything else in a sans.
avoid_when: Any body text, any TV, dense products; also avoid if the brief did not ask for 'premium' (this is now a common AI default: cream background + serif display + terracotta).
guidance: Display serif at ≥32 px with tight tracking, paired with a neutral sans body; check the pairing on the real background colour; avoid combining with the cream/terracotta palette unless the brand owns it.
source: Typography practice; observed AI default clusters

title: Monospace as identity for technical products
use_when: Developer tools, logs, terminals, code-adjacent products where monospace for data and labels reinforces the domain.
avoid_when: Long prose, consumer products, anything where monospace makes labels wider than the layout allows.
guidance: Monospace for code, IDs, timestamps, and metrics (e.g. JetBrains Mono, IBM Plex Mono, Geist Mono, Commit Mono); a compact sans for prose and navigation. Never set paragraphs in monospace.

title: Condensed display for broadcast/media
use_when: Sports, live TV, EPG and news where many titles must fit and a broadcast feel is wanted.
avoid_when: Body text, small sizes on TV (condensed faces lose legibility below ~24 sp), forms.
guidance: Condensed only for titles and channel names (e.g. Barlow Condensed, Oswald, Roboto Condensed, Archivo Narrow) at heavy weights; body and metadata in a normal-width sans with tabular figures for times.

title: Rounded friendly sans
use_when: Children, wellness, playful consumer brands, kiosks for the general public.
avoid_when: Finance, enterprise, anything where 'friendly' undermines trust; also avoid if it is only chosen because the icons are rounded.
guidance: Rounded terminals (e.g. Nunito, Quicksand for display only, Varela Round, M PLUS Rounded) with generous size; keep weights ≥500 for legibility; pair corner radius and icon style consistently with the type.

title: Neutral canvas + one accent
use_when: Application UI where colour must mean something: accent for primary actions and selection, semantic colours for feedback, everything else neutral.
avoid_when: Brand-led marketing where a dominant brand colour is the identity.
guidance: Neutral scale with a slight brand tint (not pure grey), one accent used for ≤10% of the screen, feedback colours distinct from the accent by hue family (error must not be the accent's hue). Charts get their own categorical palette. Validate every pair with tokens.py.

title: Dark canvas + accent (dark-first)
use_when: TV and media (viewing in dim rooms, OLED power), trading/monitoring consoles used for hours, developer tools; when imagery must pop.
avoid_when: Long-form reading in bright environments, forms-heavy products for the general public, print-adjacent content.
guidance: Canvas is a dark tinted neutral (not #000 unless OLED black is deliberate), surfaces step lighter with elevation, text primary ≈ 87–92% white not pure white, accent desaturated slightly for dark backgrounds, error/success re-tuned for dark contrast. On TV target ≥7:1 for body text and avoid saturated reds/oranges at large areas (bloom on cheap panels).
source: Android TV Color on TV; Material dark theme guidance

title: Dominant brand colour
use_when: Brand recognition is the goal (marketing, consumer apps, kiosks in a branded space) and the brand colour can carry large surfaces with compliant text on it.
avoid_when: Data-dense tools (colour noise), or when the brand colour fails 4.5:1 with both black and white text (then it can only be an accent).
guidance: Brand colour on large surfaces with a verified on-colour text token; a secondary neutral for content areas; do not derive the whole palette by tinting everything with the brand hue. Interactive states need visible deltas on the brand surface.

title: Duotone identity
use_when: Multi-brand differentiation where one brand needs a recognisably different colour logic from its siblings; editorial or cultural brands.
avoid_when: Semantic-heavy UI where two hues would collide with success/error meanings.
guidance: Two hues with defined roles (one for surfaces/identity, one for action/emphasis), neutrals derived from the first hue, feedback colours chosen to avoid both. Test that the pair reads for colour-blind users (deuteranopia simulation) since duotones often pick red/green-adjacent pairs.

title: Multicolour by category
use_when: Categories that users must tell apart at a glance (subjects, channels, calendars, wards) and there are ≤8 of them.
avoid_when: More than ~8 categories, or when colour would also be needed for status (conflict).
guidance: Category colours from a colour-blind-safe categorical palette, always paired with a label or icon, kept out of the action/status roles; neutrals for everything else so the categories stand out.

title: Monochrome with typographic hierarchy
use_when: Editorial, fashion, minimal tools where hierarchy comes from type and space; brands whose identity is black/white plus imagery.
avoid_when: Products that need status colour (monitoring), TV (needs stronger focus cues), or when the team cannot maintain typographic discipline.
guidance: Neutral scale only, with one reserved chromatic colour for errors and links if needed; interactive states via weight, underline, and tone; imagery provides the colour. Focus indication must be a visible ring or underline since colour is unavailable.

title: Material tonal palette (Android)
use_when: Android apps already on Material 3 / Compose, or Android TV apps using tv-material3: derive roles from a seed and let the tonal system handle contrast pairs.
avoid_when: Cross-platform brands that must look identical on iOS/web, or when dynamic colour would override brand.
guidance: Generate the scheme from the brand seed, disable dynamic colour if brand consistency is required, use container/on-container pairs rather than hand-picked hex, and verify TV variants with higher contrast (tv-material3 defaults are dark).

implementation.compose: MaterialTheme(colorScheme = lightColorScheme(...)) built from Material Theme Builder export; dynamicColor = false for brand lock.
implementation.compose-tv: androidx.tv.material3 MaterialTheme with darkColorScheme; keep surface variants for focus states.

title: Functional minimal motion
use_when: Default for application UI: motion only for state change, continuity (open/close, expand), and feedback; 120–250 ms, ease-out for entering, ease-in for leaving.
avoid_when: Brand moments (launch, onboarding) that deliberately need more; then use 'expressive' for those moments only.
guidance: Animate transform and opacity only; durations from a 3-step token scale (fast/base/slow); no motion on hover beyond colour/underline; respect prefers-reduced-motion by removing non-essential motion, not by making it faster.
source: Material motion; Apple HIG motion; WCAG 2.3.3

title: Spring-based physical motion
use_when: Gesture-driven mobile UI (sheets, swipes, drags) where motion should track the finger and settle naturally; consumer brands wanting liveliness.
avoid_when: Desktop enterprise tools, TV (springs read as lag on focus), anywhere without gestures.
guidance: Use the platform spring APIs (SwiftUI .spring, Compose spring(), Motion/Framer spring on web) with one or two named presets (snappy, gentle); interruptible and gesture-tracking; never chain springs on page load.
source: Apple HIG motion; Material motion physics

title: Focus-driven motion (TV)
use_when: TV: motion exists to show where focus is and where it went; scale/glow on focus, smooth rail scrolling to the pivot, backdrop crossfade.
avoid_when: Never elsewhere; and on TV never add decorative ambient motion that competes with focus.
guidance: Focus scale 1.05–1.1 in ≤150 ms, rail scroll ≤250 ms, backdrop crossfade 300–500 ms debounced; input must never be dropped while animating (queue focus moves); test on a low-end device for dropped frames.
source: Android TV focus system (scale 1.025/1.05/1.1); Compose for TV

title: Crossfade and shared-element continuity
use_when: Navigating from a list item to its detail where the image/title should stay anchored (poster → detail, product → PDP).
avoid_when: Data screens where the transition would delay the user, or when the shared element changes aspect ratio drastically.
guidance: Shared element for one anchor (the image) plus a crossfade for the rest; 250–350 ms; reduced-motion swaps to an instant crossfade. Use platform APIs (View Transitions API, SharedTransitionLayout, matchedGeometryEffect) not manual clones.

implementation.react: document.startViewTransition with view-transition-name on the shared image; Next.js App Router supports it with a small wrapper.

source: View Transitions API; Compose shared element; SwiftUI matchedGeometryEffect

title: Cinematic reveals (brand moments only)
use_when: Launch screens, campaign landing pages, TV app splash/attract mode: one orchestrated sequence with staggered reveals.
avoid_when: Anywhere users return to daily; on scroll for every section (scroll-triggered everything is an AI-slop marker); on low-end TV hardware.
guidance: One sequence ≤1.2 s total, transform/opacity only, plays once per session, fully skippable, and reduced-motion renders the final state immediately. Everything after the sequence uses functional motion.

title: Expressive brand motion
use_when: Consumer brands whose personality is motion (playful, energetic) and where a motion designer defines a vocabulary (easing family, bounce amount, signature transition).
avoid_when: Any professional/enterprise product; any brand without the capacity to keep the vocabulary consistent.
guidance: Define ≤3 named easings and ≤3 durations, one signature transition (e.g. a morph), apply to state changes and navigation, never to static decoration. Reduced motion falls back to crossfades.
source: Material 3 Expressive motion; brand motion practice

title: Visible focus ring (web/desktop)
use_when: All pointer+keyboard UI: a 2–3 px ring with ≥3:1 contrast against adjacent colours, offset so it is not hidden by borders, shown for :focus-visible.
avoid_when: TV (needs scale/glow because the ring is too subtle at 3 m).
guidance: One focus token (colour + width + offset) applied globally; never outline:none without a replacement; ring must remain visible on the accent surface (use a two-tone ring or offset); composite focus in tables/lists uses a cell/row highlight plus the ring on the active element.

implementation.html-css: :focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--color-focus-ring); outline-offset: 2px; } plus a box-shadow inner ring on accent surfaces.
implementation.winui: Keep the default FocusVisualPrimaryBrush/SecondaryBrush; set UseSystemFocusVisuals=True on custom controls.
implementation.wpf: Set FocusVisualStyle explicitly on custom-templated controls; the default is lost when you retemplate.

title: Scale + glow/border focus (TV)
use_when: All TV UI: focused item scales (1.05–1.1), gains a border or glow with ≥3:1 contrast, and its metadata may expand; unfocused items stay quiet.
avoid_when: Never elsewhere; and on TV never rely on colour tint alone.
guidance: Exactly one item focused at all times and it must be on screen; scale must not clip against neighbours (reserve padding = scale overflow); focus state includes a border (2–4 dp) or glow (2–32 dp elevation) plus scale so it survives any artwork; selected ≠ focused (a selected tab still needs a focus treatment); initial focus is deterministic on every screen.

implementation.compose-tv: Surface/Card from androidx.tv.material3 with scale = ScaleIndication, border = Border(...) in the focused state; use Modifier.onFocusChanged for metadata reveal.
implementation.react-native: Pressable with focus state via onFocus/onBlur; Animated scale; hasTVPreferredFocus for initial focus.
implementation.swiftui: tvOS gives .focusable() views the system lift automatically; add .hoverEffect(.lift) and custom borders only when brand demands.
implementation.react: Web-on-TV: :focus styles with transform scale + outline; spatial-navigation library sets focus, CSS shows it.

source: Android TV focus system (scale 1.025/1.05/1.1, glow 2–32 dp); tvOS HIG focus

title: Underline / weight focus for text-first UI
use_when: Editorial sites where rings would clash with the typography; links and nav items show focus with an underline/background shift plus the ring on non-text controls.
avoid_when: Applications, forms, anything with buttons and inputs as the main controls.
guidance: Text links: 2 px underline + background tint on focus (≥3:1); buttons/inputs still get the standard ring. Never remove the ring globally to protect the aesthetic.

title: Touch-only focus handling (mobile)
use_when: Native mobile and kiosk apps where there is no persistent keyboard focus; feedback is pressed state + screen-reader focus provided by the platform.
avoid_when: Any app that supports hardware keyboards, external pointers (iPadOS, Android desktop mode), or switch access without testing them.
guidance: Pressed state within 100 ms (ripple/opacity/scale), 44 pt / 48 dp targets, screen-reader focus order = visual order, and platform focus visuals left enabled for keyboard/switch users (do not disable). Kiosks: larger targets (≥ 60 px) and no hover-dependent affordances.
source: Apple HIG; Material touch feedback; kiosk accessibility practice

title: One primary action per screen
use_when: Task screens (forms, checkout, onboarding, settings) where one action completes the job; the primary is filled, secondaries are quiet.
avoid_when: Workbenches with many equal commands (toolbar pattern) or browse screens where selection is the action (focus-selects).
guidance: Exactly one filled button per view, secondaries as outlined/text, destructive actions separated and confirmed, button label is a verb phrase naming the outcome ('Save changes'), disabled only with an explanation nearby.
source: Common interaction design practice; Material button hierarchy

title: Sticky action bar
use_when: Long forms or detail pages where the primary action must stay reachable (Add to cart, Save, Continue).
avoid_when: Short screens, TV, or when the bar would cover content without a scroll padding compensation.
guidance: Bottom-fixed on mobile inside the safe area, sticky footer on desktop; content gets bottom padding equal to the bar height; the bar must not obscure a focused field (WCAG 2.4.11) so scroll the field into view above it.

title: Contextual inline actions
use_when: Content-first screens where actions belong next to the thing they act on (reply under a comment, edit next to a field, enrol beside a course).
avoid_when: Screens with one clear task; desktop tools with command bars.
guidance: Actions are visible (not hover-only), consistently placed per item type, and grouped: at most one emphasised per item. Hover-reveal is allowed only as an addition to a visible affordance and never on touch/TV.

title: Toolbar / command bar with selection-driven commands
use_when: Workbenches and tables: commands apply to the current selection, live in a persistent bar, and are mirrored by context menus and shortcuts.
avoid_when: Consumer or single-task screens; touch-first products.
guidance: Primary commands as labelled buttons, overflow into a menu, disabled (not hidden) when no selection, keyboard accelerators shown in tooltips, and the count of selected items visible near the commands.

implementation.winui: CommandBar with AppBarButton + KeyboardAccelerator; IsEnabled bound to selection.
implementation.react: Toolbar following the APG toolbar pattern (roving tabindex); disable via aria-disabled with reason in tooltip.

source: Windows command bar guidance; WAI-ARIA toolbar pattern

title: Focus is the action (TV)
use_when: TV browse/detail screens: the focused card is the call to action, SELECT opens, and detail screens expose a small row of focusable buttons (Play, Resume, Add to list) with a deterministic first focus.
avoid_when: Never on touch/pointer platforms.
guidance: No 'button-like' cards with an inner button; the whole card is focusable and selectable. Detail screen: ≤4 actions in one row, first focus on Play/Resume, LEFT/RIGHT between them, DOWN to rails. Long press or a Menu key can open secondary actions. Never require diagonal or multi-key gestures.
source: Android TV design: Cards, Buttons; tvOS HIG focus and selection

title: Floating action button (Material)
use_when: Android apps with one dominant creative action per screen (compose, add, record) that fits Material conventions.
avoid_when: iOS-first products (not idiomatic), screens with no single dominant action, or where the FAB would cover list content and the last row cannot be padded.
guidance: One FAB, labelled (extended FAB where space allows), 16 dp from edges, list content padded so the last item is not covered, hides on scroll down if it obscures content. Never use a FAB as a navigation button.

title: No decorative imagery
use_when: Operational products: imagery only where it is data (avatars, product thumbnails, charts).
avoid_when: Brand or content products where imagery is the content.
guidance: Remove stock photos, abstract blobs, and hero illustrations from working screens; empty states may use a small, meaningful illustration or none. Identity comes from type, colour, and structure.

title: Hero imagery on landing/brand pages
use_when: Landing and campaign pages where a real photograph, product render, or live demo communicates the offer better than words.
avoid_when: Dashboards, apps, article pages; and never as a default 'headline + subtitle + two buttons + screenshot' block for unrelated products.
guidance: The hero is a thesis about the product: show the actual thing (product, interface, outcome). Reserve aspect box to avoid CLS, serve responsive sources, LCP image preloaded, text contrast guaranteed by placement or scrim, and no autoplay video without a static poster and reduced-motion respect.
source: Landing page practice; Core Web Vitals

title: Poster art as primary recognition
use_when: Catalogues where the artwork is how users recognise items (films, shows, albums, courses, products).
avoid_when: Items without consistent artwork, or when text metadata is the recognition cue (documents, transactions).
guidance: One aspect ratio per rail (2:3 portrait or 16:9 landscape), title text below or revealed on focus (never over the art without a scrim), placeholders with the title text for missing art, images sized to the rendered card (no 4K posters in 200 px cards), progressive loading with a low-res or colour placeholder.

title: Immersive backdrop
use_when: Media home/detail screens on large displays where the focused/selected item's backdrop fills the screen behind text and rails.
avoid_when: Low-end devices, inconsistent artwork, or screens where users read a lot of text.
guidance: Backdrop at panel resolution max, decoded once and cached, crossfade debounced, dual scrim (left-to-right and bottom-to-top) so the text block and the rails both read; verify text contrast against the brightest backdrop in the catalogue, not the sample.
source: Android TV Immersive list; tvOS HIG

title: Functional thumbnails
use_when: Lists and grids where a small image helps recognition (products, people, files) but text carries the meaning.
avoid_when: When the thumbnail would be a generic placeholder for most items.
guidance: Fixed size per context, consistent crop (object-fit cover with a focal point), alt text that is empty when redundant with the adjacent text, lazy-loaded below the fold with intrinsic size set.

title: Data graphics as the visual layer
use_when: Analytics, monitoring, and finance where charts, sparklines, and status marks are the imagery; identity comes from the chart style.
avoid_when: Content or commerce products.
guidance: One chart palette and one mark style across the product, sparklines in tables for trends, no decorative charts (every chart answers a question), accessible alternatives (table or summary) for each chart.

title: Illustration system
use_when: Onboarding, empty states, and explanatory moments where a consistent illustration style (one stroke weight, one palette) supports comprehension; brands with an illustration language.
avoid_when: As decoration on every card/section (the 'blob and person' AI marker), or when no consistent style can be maintained.
guidance: Define the style (line, flat, isometric) once, use it in ≤4 places (onboarding, empty, error, success), keep it meaningful (depicts the task), and mark decorative instances aria-hidden.

title: Outline icon set, one weight
use_when: Most application UI: a single outline set (Lucide, Phosphor Regular, Tabler, Fluent regular) at one stroke weight and 2–3 sizes.
avoid_when: TV at small sizes (thin strokes vanish) or when the platform set is expected (SF Symbols, Material Symbols).
guidance: Icons only where they carry meaning (actions, states, object types); no icon beside every heading or list item; icon-only controls get an accessible name; sizes from tokens (16/20/24); never mix sets.

title: Filled icons for distance and touch
use_when: TV, kiosks, and touch UI where icons must read at a glance and at distance; selected states in tab bars (filled = selected).
avoid_when: Dense desktop UI where filled icons become heavy blobs.
guidance: Filled or bold-weight set at ≥24 dp (≥32 dp on TV), always with a visible label in navigation, filled/outline swap allowed only to show selection.
source: Material Symbols filled; Android TV navigation drawer icons

title: Platform icon set
use_when: Native apps: SF Symbols on Apple, Material Symbols on Android/TV, Fluent/Segoe Fluent Icons on Windows, so weight, scale, and accessibility metadata match the platform.
avoid_when: Multi-brand products needing custom glyph identity.
guidance: Use the platform set with its variable weight/fill axes rather than importing a web set; align icon weight to text weight; provide accessibility labels via the platform API.
source: SF Symbols; Material Symbols; Segoe Fluent Icons

title: Duotone icons as brand accent
use_when: Consumer brands where icons carry personality and a second tone (brand tint) is part of the identity.
avoid_when: Dense tools, TV, or where the second tone would fail non-text contrast.
guidance: Duotone in feature/marketing contexts; in functional UI revert to a single-tone variant of the same set so navigation stays crisp. Verify the secondary tone is decorative (meaning must survive in monochrome).

title: Text-only, no icon system
use_when: Editorial, fashion, and typographic brands where icons would dilute the identity; navigation and actions are words.
avoid_when: Applications with many repeated actions, mobile tab bars, TV.
guidance: Words for everything except universally understood glyphs (search, close, menu on narrow widths); use weight and case for hierarchy; this is a deliberate stance and must be applied consistently.

title: Custom glyph set
use_when: Established brands with an icon language and the capacity to maintain it (grid, stroke, corner rules, ≥60 glyphs).
avoid_when: Any team without an icon designer; the result is inconsistent metaphors. Start from a system set and customise a handful of brand-critical glyphs instead.
guidance: Define the grid (24 px, 2 px stroke or filled), test at every token size, ship as SVG sprites/vector drawables with names that map to meaning, and keep a fallback mapping to a system set for missing glyphs.

title: Minimal metadata
use_when: Browsing and consumption surfaces where one line (title) or two (title + one fact) is enough to choose.
avoid_when: Decision-heavy contexts (comparison, operations) where hidden facts force extra clicks.
guidance: Title plus at most one secondary line; everything else on the detail screen. On TV, reveal one more line on focus rather than showing it always.

title: Moderate metadata with a hierarchy
use_when: Lists and cards where 3–4 facts help the choice (price, rating, date, status) and can be typographically ranked.
avoid_when: When facts exceed four (use a table or detail) or when only one matters.
guidance: Rank facts: title, then the deciding fact (price/status), then supporting facts in a muted style; status via badge + text; align numbers; no icon per fact.

title: Rich metadata (operational)
use_when: Operations: many attributes per record visible at once (tables, ledgers, tickets), with sorting/filtering on any of them.
avoid_when: Consumer browsing, mobile, TV.
guidance: Columns with user-controlled visibility and order, consistent formatting per type (dates, currency, IDs in monospace), status as text+colour, truncation with full value on focus/hover and in the detail pane.

title: Focus-revealed metadata (TV)
use_when: TV rails: unfocused cards show title only (or nothing over art); the focused card or a fixed detail strip shows synopsis, year, duration, rating.
avoid_when: Never for touch/pointer; and on TV avoid when the reveal reflows the rail (use a fixed strip instead).
guidance: Reveal into reserved space (a fixed detail area above the rails or an expanded card whose height is pre-allocated) so rows never jump; keep the reveal text ≥24 sp; delay the reveal ~150 ms so quick scrubbing does not flash text.
source: Android TV cards and immersive list; tvOS focus behaviour

title: Inline badges and status chips
use_when: Status, category, or count must be scannable in lists and headers (Open/Closed, New, 3 unread).
avoid_when: As decoration on everything; when more than two badges per item appear, the design has become noisy.
guidance: Pill only for status/category/count; text inside the pill (never colour only); ≤2 per item; consistent colour mapping across the product; not clickable unless it is a filter.

title: No card containers (dividers and spacing)
use_when: Most screens: sections separated by headings, spacing, and hairline dividers; cards reserved for genuinely tappable objects.
avoid_when: When the item boundary is itself the target and items are visually heterogeneous (then a card is right).
guidance: Remove nested rounded rectangles; group with whitespace and a heading; use a single hairline between rows; only wrap something in a card when it needs its own boundary for tapping, dragging, or elevation. This is the biggest single lever against generic AI layouts.
source: Interface design practice; observed AI default patterns

title: Flat tiles
use_when: Grids of equal items where a tonal background and small radius delineate the item without shadows.
avoid_when: Items with varying heights (tiles then look ragged) or when nothing about the item is tappable.
guidance: One surface tone step above canvas, 4–8 px radius, no border unless contrast between tile and canvas is below ~1.2:1, consistent inner padding from the spacing scale.

title: List rows
use_when: Homogeneous items on phones and in side panels: full-width rows with leading image/icon, title, secondary line, trailing meta, hairline dividers.
avoid_when: Items whose image is the recognition cue (use tiles/posters).
guidance: Row height from the density token (48–72 dp), whole row tappable with one accessible name, trailing chevron only when it navigates, swipe actions mirrored by a visible menu.

title: Portrait poster cards (2:3)
use_when: Films, series, books, courses with portrait key art; rails or grids of 5–7 visible items on TV.
avoid_when: Landscape-only art (episodes, live channels, sports) or when titles must be read without the art.
guidance: Fixed 2:3 ratio, title below the art (not over it) unless the art contains the title reliably, placeholder with title text, scale on focus with reserved margin. On TV about 6 per row at 960 dp width with 20 dp gutters.
source: Android TV cards (standard card sizes); streaming conventions

title: Landscape media cards (16:9)
use_when: Episodes, live channels, sports, continue-watching rows, video tutorials: landscape thumbnails with a progress bar and duration.
avoid_when: Portrait-native art collections.
guidance: Fixed 16:9, progress bar inside the art bottom edge with a scrim, duration/remaining badge with text, channel logo for live, 4 per row on TV at 960 dp with 20 dp gutters, title below.

title: Bordered cards
use_when: Settings pages, integration lists, plan pickers: discrete objects on a light canvas where a 1 px border (≥3:1) delineates without elevation.
avoid_when: Nested inside other cards or panels; on dark themes where borders vanish (use tonal steps).
guidance: Border token with measured contrast, 6–8 px radius, header row with title and one action, body with a clear hierarchy; selectable cards (plans) use a stronger border + check mark, never colour alone.
